precepts.text: The Lord turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends; the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before, and blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning. Endure to the end and God shall restore everything.
precepts.point: Only a spiritual man can understand that. Joseph was on another level of understanding: he sat back and reflected on all that happened to him and knew it was God's divine plan. He may not have understood it while he was in the midst of it, but going through the years of plenty and famine he realized his purpose, and God set that whole thing up.

note.label: Joseph in Egypt: Then & Now

precepts.why:
Endure to the end, and God shall restore everything. Job is the proof: “And the Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before.”

His brethren and sisters and old acquaintances came and ate bread with him, “and they bemoaned him, and comforted him over all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him.” “So the Lord blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning: for he had fourteen thousand sheep, and six thousand camels, and a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses.” He had seven sons and three daughters, Jemima, Kezia and Keren-happuch, “And in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job.”

Joseph's life ran the same way: sold, slandered, imprisoned, and then made ruler over Egypt, with his brethren falling down before his face. The latter end was greater than the beginning. Whatever you are suffering, endure it; God turns the captivity of those who hold on, and blesses their latter end more than their beginning.

precepts.text: Now mine eye seeth thee, wherefore I abhor myself and repent in dust and ashes. Job repented for justifying himself instead of the Lord.
precepts.point: The three men ceased to answer Job because he was righteous in his own eyes, and Elihu's wrath was kindled because Job justified himself rather than God. Job said he was not weak like Adam. That was his flaw: he was over-righteous.

note.label: Fighting Satan - the War Within

precepts.why:
Job ends where chapter 32 began. There the three men ceased to answer him “because he was righteous in his own eyes”, and Elihu was angry “because he justified himself rather than God.” Here Job says, “I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.”

Job hated himself and repented. He repented for justifying himself and not God, for being righteous in his own eyes. He had said, I am righteous, this is not supposed to happen to me; I made a covenant with mine eyes, I don't look at other women, I am not weak like Adam, I don't hide sin in my bosom. That was his flaw. He was over-righteous, and the Lord did not like it.

In his own eyes Job did not look at it as though there was a reason God was doing this, that God was trying to make him better. In his mind it was, I am righteous, I am not like this person or that person. So the Bible says, “Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself?” That person who tries to act over-righteous just ends up looking fake; nobody knows everything and nobody is perfect.

This is the war within, the war nobody sees. Everything Job suffered before was physical, but Satan was attacking his mind too. The Lord used what Job went through to show him what was inside himself, and that is what Satan's attacks do: they show you things inside yourself. Through all of it Job was made perfect, and he came out of it repenting in dust and ashes, justifying God instead of himself.

precepts.text: We are judged by our words, for the Most High hears all our words and even our thoughts, so nothing can be withholden from Him.
precepts.point: Dust and ashes refer to the custom our forefathers had of putting ashes on the head as a sign of sorrow and repentance.

note.label: Job 42: The Lord Turned the Captivity of Job

precepts.why:
Job confesses, “I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.” This is a little thing in the scriptures to take heed to. Christ says, “For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.”

We are judged by our words, and the Most High hears all our words and even our thoughts, so nothing can be withholden from him. The hatred or the private spirit a man carries cannot be hidden from him; he knows the inward parts of men. Job had heard of him by the hearing of the ear, but now his eye sees him, and so he abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes, the custom our forefathers had of putting ashes on the head as a sign of sorrow and repentance.

precepts.text: Job was a perfect man, which is why the Most High held him up as the one who spoke rightly while his friends did not.
precepts.point: This is how the priesthood worked, all the way from Leviticus and the five books throughout history: we brought the sacrifice to the Levites and priests and they did it on our behalf, and if a man did not bring his sacrifice, the Most High would deal with him and what he did would not be forgiven. Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the Most High commanded, and He accepted Job.

note.label: Job 42: The Lord Turned the Captivity of Job

precepts.why:
The Lord tells Eliphaz the Temanite, “ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.” Why Job? Because “that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.” Job was a perfect man, so the Most High held him up as the one who spoke rightly while his friends did not.

Throughout the book Job's three friends dealt wrongly with him after his children were killed and everything was taken, so they did not deal righteously as their brother Job did. That is why the sacrifice for their sin, seven bullocks and seven rams, had to be brought to Job, the righteous one in the situation, and Job would pray for them, lest the Most High deal with them after their folly.

This is how the priesthood worked, all the way from Leviticus and the five books throughout history: we brought the sacrifice to the Levites and priests and they did it on our behalf, and if a man did not bring his sacrifice, the Most High would deal with him and what he did would not be forgiven. Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the Most High commanded, and he accepted Job.

precepts.text: Confess your faults one to another and pray one for another, for the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much, and it was Job's righteous prayer that spared his friends.
precepts.point: Then all his brethren, sisters, and former acquaintances came and ate bread with him, bemoaned him, and comforted him over all the evil the Most High had brought upon him, and every man gave him a piece of money and an earring of gold. After his captivity was turned his friends returned as well.

note.label: Job 42: The Lord Turned the Captivity of Job

precepts.why:
“And the Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends”. James shows why that prayer worked: “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.”

It was not the prayer alone that availed, but the prayer of a righteous man. It was Job's righteous prayer that spared his friends, and the Most High deals with those that are dealing in righteousness. When Job prayed for them, the Lord turned his captivity and gave him twice as much as he had before, and after his captivity was turned his brethren, his sisters and his former acquaintances returned as well.

precepts.text: Satan comes before the Most High from going to and fro in the earth, and the whole point of the trial was to see whether Job would curse the Most High to His face once the hedge was removed.
precepts.point: The purpose of the trial was to see whether Job would fix himself and stay faithful or curse the Most High. The same thing happens to us: we endure to the end as Job did, and at some point the Most High will turn the captivity of the Israelites who kept the commandments and repay them for all their righteousness, far more than double the houses, families, cars, and jobs we have now, giving us much more in the kingdom.

note.label: Job 42: The Lord Turned the Captivity of Job

precepts.why:
To see why the Lord blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning, go back to where the trial began. “And the Lord said unto Satan, Whence comest thou? Then Satan answered the Lord, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” The Lord asks, “Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?”

Satan answers, “Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?” Then: “But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face.” That was the whole point of the trial: to see whether Job would fix himself and stay faithful, or curse the Most High to his face once the hedge was removed.

Job stayed faithful to the Most High through the whole trial, and that is why he received much more than he had in the beginning: fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, a thousand she asses, seven sons and three daughters, and a hundred and forty years to see his sons and his sons' sons, even four generations.

precepts.text: Here is the patience and the faith of the saints, for we endure to the end just as Job endured his trial.
precepts.point: The purpose of the trial was to see whether Job would fix himself and stay faithful or curse the Most High. The same thing happens to us: we endure to the end as Job did, and at some point the Most High will turn the captivity of the Israelites who kept the commandments and repay them for all their righteousness, far more than double the houses, families, cars, and jobs we have now, giving us much more in the kingdom.

note.label: Job 42: The Lord Turned the Captivity of Job

precepts.why:
“Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.” Job endured his trial, and we endure to the end as Job did, keeping the commandments and the faith.

The same thing happens to us. At some point the Most High will turn the captivity of the Israelites who kept the commandments and repay them for all their righteousness, far more than double the houses, families, cars, and jobs we have now, giving us much more in the kingdom, just as he blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning.

precepts.text: The Lord blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning with sheep, camels, oxen, and she asses.
precepts.point: Job is an example. Job was tried by the Lord in the first chapters, and he was blessed in his latter end, living to see four generations of his children.

precepts.why: “So Job died, being old and full of days.” That is the end of a man who kept God’s laws and was blessed: old and full of days, having seen his children’s children to four generations. Plenty of benefits come with keeping God’s laws, and peace upon Israel.

points: Job lived an hundred and forty years, and saw his sons, and his sons' sons, even four generations. The generation here is talking about his descendants: your son, your grandson, your great grandson, your great great grandson. That is genealogical generation.

So when we read Genesis 15, is the fourth generation talking about descendants? Seventy souls went into Egypt. A fourth generation genealogically does not equal four hundred years, so something else is being said there.
